parsed.summary: The writer rose angry with his boy for lying long abed and forgetting his lute, then spent the morning at his office and went to the 'Change and home to dinner. In the afternoon at Gresham College he found great pleasure in hearing Commissioner Pett turn and wind Mr. Castle over his ship draught, having himself studied the subject of late. He worked late at his office to his content, though he notes the ado of getting himself to come home to business or to stay there. That evening a letter from Plymouth told him two ships, the Leopard and another, were lost by running aground and a Dutch fleet had gone thither, which he reckoned most sad news. On coming home that night he was much troubled to hear his canary bird of three or four years was dead.

parsed.summary: The writer rose and went to White Hall and the Lords' House about getting a privy seal for felling the King's timber for the navy. At the 'Change, he met more ill news on top of the previous night's. A released Frenchman told him of a Dutch man-of-war of thirty-six guns, with seven more like ships, taken off the North Foreland, which he called a strange attempt. He noted the easterly wind that would keep the English force at Portsmouth from coming but carry the Dutch home, and prayed God to preserve them and pardon calling the enemy contemptible. He then dined at home with Mr. Hollyard, worked at the office until after 11 at night, and went home to supper and bed.

canon.summary: The writer rose and went to White Hall and the Lords' House about getting a privy seal for felling the King's timber for the navy. At the 'Change, he met more ill news on top of the previous night's. A released Frenchman told him of a Dutch man-of-war of thirty-six guns, with seven more like ships, taken off the North Foreland, which he called a strange attempt. parsed.summary: Mr. Creed called Pepys up to talk about Tangier business, and afterwards Jane Welsh, Mr. Jervas his maid, came to say she had left her master and would stick to her sweetheart Harbing, a poor little fellow. Pepys tried to dissuade her, took her by boat to the Falcon, and talked with her for an hour or two, urging her to stay out her time, but she said it was her fortune to have this man even if it meant her ruine, which he called strange and stupid. He then dined at Mr. Povy's, went to Lord Bellasses' and White Hall, delivered a letter to the Duke of Yorke, and talked with Mr. Slingsby about the Mint, coinage and the law against exporting bullion, which he came to see as a folly and an injury. He visited the sick Sir J. Minnes, was shown Mrs. Turner's Rocke, and ended the day working late at his office before supper and bed.

He then dined at Mr. Povy's, went about business with Lord Bellasses, the Duke of Albemarle and the Duke of York, and talked with Mr. Slingsby about the Mint and coinage, coming to understand that the law against exporting bullion is a folly and an injury. He visited the still-sick Sir J. Minnes, was shown Mrs. Turner's Rocke, and ended working late at his office before supper and bed.

They held up their hands crying 'What shall we do?', and the Lord Treasurer asked why people would not lend money and trust the King; they got no other answer, which Pepys called one of the saddest things. He went home vexed, found women merry at Lady Batten's where Lady Pen flung him on the bed, and was as merry as he could be, though vexed, before supper and bed.

parsed.summary: Rising at five, the diarist went to Chelsea, where after all his fears the Lord Privy Seal passed his Tangier Privy Seal at first reading and was very civil to him. Much joyed, he returned to London, told Povy, dined pleasantly at Trinity House, and watched Florence poison experiments on animals at Gresham College. Povy then took him away and gave him exceeding discouragements about getting money, fearing Backewell had a design to have the thing forced upon himself, which put him into a cruel melancholy. He consulted with Creed, and then met Mr. Warren, from whom he feared his hopes would fail. He noted the troubles would be seen at worst in a day or two, and went to bed by 10 or 11 with his head aching.

Walking with Povy, he was given exceeding discouragements about getting money and warned that Backewell may have a design to have the thing forced upon himself. This put him into a cruel melancholy at the thought of losing what he had so near, though he still hoped something from the morrow; after consulting Creed and meeting Mr. Warren, whose hopes he feared would fail, he went to bed with an aching head, trusting the worst would be seen in a day or two.

He drinks and talks with Mary at the Harp and Ball, and stops further talk when she says she lately lived at his neighbour Mr. Knightly's. He remarks that he has not kept summer days by daylight and resolves to try for a month before going to supper and bed.

parsed.summary: Pepys walked to Greenwich, pleased to time his walk with his minute watch, then dined with fellow officers at Sir W. Hickes's, a run-down house where he was given the meanest dinner he ever saw. He was pleased only by a fine Van Dyke picture of the Queen-Mother. Returning home, he found his wife had been out all day, nobody knowing where, which troubled him since it was late and cold. He went to supper at Mr. Pen's mother's, where his wife later arrived after being with Captain Cocke all day. After supper he and Mr. Pen argued over a French song's words for over an hour, almost angry, and parted unsatisfied before going home to bed.

On returning home he walked with Mr. Pen, who told ill-told tales of France, and found his wife had been abroad all day, nobody knowing where, which troubled him on a late, cold evening. He later supped at Pen's mother's, where his wife arrived, having been with Captain Cocke all day, and he had no stomach to eat. After supper he and Pen disputed for over an hour about a French song's words, almost angry and unsatisfied, before going home to bed.

He dined with Sheriff Hooker, then at the Pope's Head Tavern Captain Cocke signed a £2,000 bill of imprest, which gladdened his heart, and Sir W. Warren arranged £100 and an insurance business. After seeking the Duke of Albemarle's advice and concluding the insurance plan with Lord Brunckner late at night, he went home with his mind in great rest and to bed.
